newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Japan PM discusses ASEAN, China in Malaysia visit.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM discusses ASEAN, China in Malaysia visit.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Wednesday held talks with his Malaysian counterpart, during which he discussed regional issues such as tightening ASEAN ties and the growing presence of China.

The Japanese leader wrapped up a two-hour meeting with Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad after arriving on Wednesday on the second leg of a tour to five Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) members.
Security measures were tightened for the Japanese leader's visit, which comes amid a three-week-old hostage crisis at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, Peru.

During the meeting with Mahathir, Hashimoto suggested that there should be more regular meetings between ASEAN leaders and Tokyo, Abdul Kadir Mohamad, secretary-general of Malaysia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, told a news briefing.
Mahathir told the Japanese leader he would consult other ASEAN leaders on that request, Abdul Kadir said.
Malaysia currently chairs ASEAN, which is celebrating its 30th anniversary this year.

Abdul Kadir said Hashimoto said Tokyo was positive to the idea of Burma's eventual entry into the Southeast Asian group. But the Japanese prime minister said he was aware of concerns in his country about human rights issues.
ASEAN has said it will admit Burma, Laos and Cambodia as full members at the same time, but has stopped short of saying when that will take place.
Burma's proposed inclusion into the group has been controversial because of the military crackdown in that country on the pro-democracy movement.
On China's growing presence in Asia, Mahathir told his Japanese counterpart that "Malaysia feels a policy of friendship is better than a policy of containment," Abdul Kadir said.
Hashimoto's Asia-Pacific strategy is expected to be underpinned by increasing economic cooperation with ASEAN members and containing China's growing influence in the region.
On bilateral matters, Malaysia has reiterated its interest in continuing to emulate Japan's economic development, Abdul Kadir said.

As chair of the Group of 15 developing countries, Malaysia has asked Japan to arrange regular forums with the Group of Seven developed countries on issues which affect the developing world, Abdul Kadir said.
For example, Malaysia wants to be involved in issues such as the strengthening of the yen, which has raised its yen-denominated debt level, he said.

Japan is Malaysia's largest trading partner, accounting for 20 percent of its overall global trade. In 1995, Malaysia's trade with Japan stood at 76.5 billion ringgit ($30.35 billion), up from 31.6 billion ringgit in 1990.
The Japanese leader visited Brunei on Tuesday and is due to call on leaders in Indonesia, Singapore and Vietnam. He toured two other ASEAN members, Thailand and the Philippines, last year.

After a brief welcoming ceremony at parliament on Wednesday, Hashimoto, who appeared to be wearing a bullet-proof vest under his suit jacket, led a 14-member delegation in bilateral talks with their Malaysian counterparts.

Malaysian police, armed with M-16's, lined the main highway leading from the international airport to the capital city. Hand-held metal detectors were used at Parliament Square, the site of the welcoming ceremony. ($1 = 2.52 ringgit)
